fixes.explanation: Paul, the apostle, calls it straight: "And you are proud!" (1 Corinthians 5:2). Imagine pulling a tray of charcoal out of the oven and doing a victory lap. I think that's why Paul's next question lands so hard, because he says they should have been stricken with grief.

Right. Paul says he wasn't including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters (1 Corinthians 5:10). Staying away from all of them would mean leaving this world, and Paul says so. His point is narrower than that.

Close, but Paul isn't holding off. He says he has "…already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present." (1 Corinthians 5:3). He's absent in body but present in spirit, as he puts it. So the judgment is already made.
True! Paul asks, "Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" (1 Corinthians 5:6). Leaven doesn't stay in one corner. It works through the whole batch.

Not this time. Paul asks, "Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" (1 Corinthians 5:6). He's saying a little leaven reaches the whole batch. It doesn't stay in one spot.

Tabernacles is a feast name too, friend, but Paul doesn't use it in this verse. He writes, "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed." (1 Corinthians 5:7). The feast whose lamb he names is Passover, and Christ is that lamb. Keep that picture in mind.

Yes! Paul says to keep the feast with "…the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth." (1 Corinthians 5:8). That's the opposite of the malice and wickedness in the old bread. Sincerity and truth are what he says belong at this feast.

Not quite, friend. Paul says, "…anyone who claims to be a brother…" and lives that way (1 Corinthians 5:11). What marks the person is that claim together with the conduct he lists. How often someone visits isn't what Paul mentions.
